steps.title: A poison message
steps.caption: m-13 has a field the handler cannot parse: it fails, comes back and fails again, and the rest wait.
steps.body: `m-13` carries a field the handler does not expect, so the handler throws and never acknowledges the message. The broker makes it available again and delivers it again, and its **receive count** climbs to 1, 2, 3 with the same error each time: a retry cannot fix a failure that is in the message or in the code. This queue delivers in order, so `m-14`, `m-15` and `m-16` wait behind it. In an unordered queue they would get through, but each redelivery of `m-13` would still burn consumer capacity.

steps.title: Park it after 3 receives
steps.caption: After 3 failed receives the broker parks m-13 in the dead-letter queue, and the queue flows again.
steps.body: The source queue has a dead-letter policy with a **maximum receive count** of 3. Instead of delivering `m-13` a fourth time, the broker moves it to the **dead-letter queue** together with what it knows: the reason (receive limit reached), the receive count and the queue it came from. The source queue flows again, and `m-14`, `m-15` and `m-16` are handled and saved.

steps.title: Alarm, then inspect
steps.caption: Depth 1 in the dead-letter queue raises an alarm. An engineer reads m-13 and fixes the handler.
steps.body: The dead-letter queue now holds one message, and an alarm on *depth > 0* pages the on-call engineer. Without that alarm a dead-letter queue is silent data loss: nothing consumes it, and many brokers delete parked messages when their retention runs out. The engineer reads `m-13` without removing it, matches it with the handler's error log and finds the cause: the handler rejects any field it does not know. The message is valid and the bug is in the consumer, so the fix is a new handler version.

steps.title: Redrive
steps.caption: After the fix, m-13 is redriven to the source queue and saved. The dead-letter queue is empty again.
steps.body: Only after the fix is deployed does the engineer **redrive** `m-13`: it re-enters the source queue as a new delivery with a fresh receive count, handler v2 saves it, and the dead-letter queue is empty again. It is saved after `m-14` to `m-16`, because parking a message gives up its place in the order. A redriven message can also repeat work that was partly done before it failed, so the consumer must be **idempotent**. A message that is invalid for good is archived or discarded on purpose instead, not left to expire.
